excerpt: A letter of protection lets you get medical treatment now and pay from your settlement later. How they work in Georgia and South Carolina.
keyTakeaways: A letter of protection (LOP) is a written agreement between your attorney and a medical provider that guarantees payment from your settlement proceeds, allowing you to receive treatment without upfront costs. LOPs are common in Georgia and South Carolina personal injury cases where victims lack health insurance or face coverage gaps. Georgia's hospital lien law (O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470) and South Carolina's equivalent (S.C. Code § 44-63-10) create separate statutory lien rights. Insurance companies may attack LOPs by arguing provider bias. Attorneys can negotiate LOP balances down 20-40% after settlement.

faqs.question: What is a letter of protection in a personal injury case?
faqs.answer: A letter of protection (LOP) is a written agreement between your attorney and a medical provider guaranteeing that the provider will be paid from the proceeds of your personal injury settlement or verdict. The LOP allows you to receive medical treatment without paying out of pocket while your case is pending.

faqs.question: Is a letter of protection legally binding?
faqs.answer: Yes. An LOP is a contractual agreement that obligates you to pay the medical provider from your settlement proceeds. If your case is unsuccessful and you recover nothing, you may still owe the medical bills.

faqs.question: Do all doctors accept letters of protection?
faqs.answer: No. Many doctors and medical facilities are selective about which LOPs they accept. Providers are more likely to accept an LOP from an attorney they have an established professional relationship with and trust to resolve the case.

faqs.question: How do insurance companies use letters of protection against me?
faqs.answer: Insurance companies may argue that doctors treating you under an LOP have a financial incentive to exaggerate your injuries or recommend unnecessary treatment. Your attorney can counter this by presenting objective medical evidence and pointing out that the doctor's professional reputation depends on honest assessments.

faqs.question: Can my attorney negotiate the medical bills under an LOP?
faqs.answer: Yes. Attorneys routinely negotiate reductions of 20-40% on LOP balances, which directly increases your take-home settlement amount.

faqs.question: What is the difference between an LOP and a medical lien?
faqs.answer: An LOP is a voluntary agreement arranged by your attorney before treatment begins. A medical lien is a statutory right that hospitals and providers can assert after treatment. In Georgia, hospital liens are governed by O.C.G.A. § 44-14-470. In South Carolina, S.C. Code § 44-63-10 controls hospital liens.
